clue.text: Argentinian perhaps showing her composure? Quite the opposite!

blocks.note: the opposite of her, the female possessive, is the male one
the opposite of calm composure is alarm

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a cool Argentinian woman is keeping her calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the opposite!' tells you to swap each of her and composure for its opposite, giving HIS PANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentina is Spanish-speaking, so an Argentinian is one example of a Spanish-heritage person from Latin America.

clue.text: H8 peak

blocks.note: taken as written
the number written out in words

explanation.walkthrough: H8 looks like a grid reference or a pencil grade; read it as H followed by the word for 8.
explanation.definitionFit: The height of something is its highest point or top level, as in the height of fashion.

clue.text: Unusual, externally coy, cheap and nasty

indicators.note: externally says the second word sits on the outside, wrapping round the first

blocks.note: coy means bashful or reserved
unusual means strange or peculiar

explanation.surface: Someone is unusually bashful on the outside but is in fact cheap and nasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy goods are badly made from poor materials, so they are low in quality and price.

clue.text: Indisposed at sea, when heading out

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, and out tells you to drop it

blocks.note: a ship at sea is out on the water under way

explanation.surface: A passenger feels poorly while the ship is out on the water and heading away from port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' reads as a seasickness detail but supplies SAILING, which loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ailing is unwell or sickly, just as an indisposed person is slightly ill.

clue.text: Commercial for Asian flower contest

blocks.note: a flower in crosswords is something that flows, a river; this one runs through Pakistan
a trial is a test or competition

explanation.surface: An advert is being made to promote an Asian flower show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; read it as flow-er, a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial relates to trade and manufacturing, which overlaps with the business sense of commercial.

clue.text: Write illegibly as a result of s-stroke

blocks.note: the letter written out before the hyphen
the front crawl is a swimming stroke

explanation.surface: Someone's handwriting has become unreadable after they suffered a stroke, with a stammer in the clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The stuttered s- is a separate S; stroke means a swimming style, not an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrawl is to scribble messily, producing handwriting that others struggle to read.

clue.text: Personal appeal — playing harmonicas not on!

indicators.note: not on says that pair of letters is removed from the fodder
playing suggests letters moving about and being rearranged like notes in a tune

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A busker's charm is that he refuses to play the harmonica.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove O and N from HARMONICAS, then rearrange the remaining eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is a magnetic charm that draws other people to someone, an individual attractiveness.

clue.text: Spot on about caricatures? No sir!

indicators.note: No tells you to take away the letters of the word sir from the fodder
about suggests letters turned around and moved into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether cartoons are exactly right, and is firmly told no, sir.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove S, I and R from CARICATURES and shuffle what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot on is an informal phrase meaning exactly right, precise or correct.

clue.text: Mercy from Lenin admitting end of regime on country borders

indicators.note: end of picks out only the final letter of the next word
admitting means letting in, so the name holds the other piece inside it
the borders of a word are its outermost letters, first and last
in a down clue, on means placed after and below the previous piece

blocks.note: the Russian revolutionary leader
the final letter of regime
the first and last letters of country

explanation.surface: A historian wonders whether Lenin ever showed clemency at the end of a regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue means the second piece goes below the first; the country's borders are just its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Leniency is gentle, forgiving treatment of wrongdoers, close to showing compassion or clemency.

clue.text: Strong-willed woman caused royal din

indicators.note: caused suggests something made or brought about, so the words are reworked into another form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A determined woman made a great fuss among the royals.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iron Lady was the nickname of Margaret Thatcher, UK prime minister 1979-90.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron lady is a tough, uncompromising woman, a phrase made famous as Thatcher's nickname.

clue.text: Tintin's dance

blocks.note: a tin is a container for food, also called a can
the second half of the name gets the same swap; the 's is just a link
the whole name is read as two halves, the comic-book reporter only being surface

explanation.surface: The boy reporter from the comic books has a favourite dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Tintin is the Belgian comic-book reporter; split his name in two and swap each half for a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The cancan is a high-kicking French music-hall routine performed by a line of dancers.

clue.text: Fellow involved in robbery is a pleasure-seeker

indicators.note: involved in means caught up inside, so one word is placed within the other

blocks.note: a heist is a robbery
a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A man caught up in a robbery turns out to be in it purely for kicks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' looks like any man, but here it is the academic title for a college teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist lives to enjoy himself, putting the pursuit of enjoyment above all else.

clue.text: Enter feature in Brighton church

blocks.note: Brighton, an English seaside resort, is known for its long pleasure pier
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A notice invites visitors to come into a notable church in Brighton.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce something is to go into or through it, making a way in.

clue.text: Perhaps Victoria, Elizabeth and Mary finally get writing materials

indicators.note: finally keeps just the last letter of the name before it

blocks.note: Victoria is a London railway terminus, so perhaps marks it as an example
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth
the final letter of Mary

explanation.surface: Three queens of England, Victoria, Elizabeth and Mary, finally receive pens and paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The list of queens tempts a royal reading, but Victoria is the London station.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationery is the general term for paper, envelopes, pens and other supplies used for correspondence.

clue.text: School working at hit crime novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is busy at school working on a hit crime novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, completing 'crime novel', but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Arithmetic is sums done in class, the calculations pupils show as their working.

clue.text: Cosmetic for small mark under cheek

indicators.note: in a down clue, under means placed below and so after the next word

blocks.note: lip is impudence, as is cheek
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a tick is a check mark

explanation.surface: Someone applies make-up to cover a small blemish on the cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheek reads as a part of the face, but it means sauciness here.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipstick is a coloured make-up applied to the mouth, one of the most common cosmetics.

clue.text: Hot and bothered at first in Dubai — moving, but not far!

definitions.text: Hot and bothered at first in Dubai — moving, but not far!

indicators.note: at first keeps the opening letter of each of the preceding words
moving means the letters shift from their places into new ones

blocks.note: the first letters of these three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flustered expat in Dubai is relocating, but only a short distance.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: the capital of the UAE is a short drive from Dubai, a hot place to move to.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of the United Arab Emirates lies close to Dubai, so moving there is not going far.

clue.text: The man's in a joint that's sticky

indicators.note: in places the first part inside the phrase that follows

blocks.note: taken as written
a dive is a seedy bar or club, informally a joint
the man is he, so the man's is he's

explanation.surface: A man is stuck in a sticky situation in some joint.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint looks anatomical or like carpentry; here it is slang for a cheap bar.
explanation.definitionFit: An adhesive substance, such as glue, sticks things together, so it is tacky to the touch.

clue.text: Home clue for state is offensive

blocks.note: at home means in
a two-word cryptic clue: the second word rearranged, as the first word signals, makes state

explanation.surface: A setter's clue for the word 'state' is considered rude.
explanation.walkthrough: BAD TASTE works as a mini clue: 'bad' is an anagram signal and TASTE rearranges to STATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in bad taste is vulgar or improper and likely to upset people.

clue.text: Don't go to bed — party wildly with us right away!

indicators.note: right gives the letter R, and away tells you to send it off
wildly suggests letters running out of control into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation not to sleep but to come and celebrate wildly with friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from PARTY, add US, and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay up is to remain awake late instead of retiring for the night.

clue.text: Tries to present a bit of thrush as agony

indicators.note: a bit of says the letters needed are a piece lifted from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to describe an infection as excruciating.
explanation.walkthrough: Thrush here may be the bird or the infection; either way only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Has a go is an idiom meaning attempts, so it swaps directly for tries.

clue.text: Spirited and fit? Yes, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements the letters could take

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a person is lively and healthy, and gets a hesitant yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A feisty person is lively, determined and full of fight, which is to say full of spirit.

clue.text: Not expected to be thrown back in abandoned dustbin

indicators.note: in says the letters are sitting inside the following words
thrown back means read in the opposite direction, right to left

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Something surprising is found, tossed back into an old bin.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sudden happens without warning, so it comes unforeseen and unanticipated.

clue.text: Scarf suggestion for competitive event

blocks.note: first meaning: Cockney slang for the face, which the word Scarf suggests by sounding like the film Scarface
second meaning: the annual rowing race between Oxford and Cambridge on the Thames

explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang BOAT RACE means face, and 'Scarf' hints at scar plus face. The Boat Race is the Oxford v Cambridge rowing contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford and Cambridge rowing contest is a famous annual sporting fixture, and its name is rhyming slang for face.

clue.text: Like this list of letters?

blocks.note: surface reading: similar to an inventory of correspondence
setter's reading: list means lean or slope, so these are letters that slant, as in a sloping typeface

explanation.walkthrough: List is a noun in the surface, but here it is the nautical verb for leaning to one side.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type slopes to the right, so its characters lean, and the clue itself may be set that way.

clue.text: Yankee into nearest lost decade

indicators.note: lost suggests the letters have gone astray and must be found in a new order
into tells you to put the first piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An American was drawn into the closest thing to a wasted decade.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters split into two words with the Yankee letter between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A decade is a period of ten years, so the phrase defines it exactly.

clue.text: Kevin's juggling daggers!

indicators.note: juggling tosses things into the air so they land in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Kevin is performing a circus act, tossing sharp blades in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Daggers are short pointed blades used for stabbing, a kind of cutting weapon.

clue.text: Extremely silly Mozart's first fake composition

indicators.note: extremely keeps the extremes, the first and last letters of the word
first keeps only the opening letter of the name before it

blocks.note: the first and last letters of silly
the first letter of Mozart
phony means fake or not genuine

explanation.surface: A very silly piece of music is passed off as Mozart's first work.
explanation.definitionFit: A symphony is an extended orchestral work, one type of musical composition.
